STEAL THESE

Nine workflows and prompts from this week’s three editions.

LET AN AGENT DRIVE YOUR COMPUTER

 * Codex handles errands. Seven staffers on the tasks they hand off to AI, including calendar upkeep, Verizon support chats, listing items for sale, troubleshooting a slow laptop, and transferring internet service. The list https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * A four-step deck workflow. Douglas Brundage designs two or three reference slides, hammers out copy with Codex, has it build the full deck in Google Slides, and saves his edits as rules for next time. The steps https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * A “don’t touch the mouse” signal. When Codex is controlling his computer, a stray click from Randy Counsman would derail the agent’s work, so he has Codex put a 🖥️ in the title of whichever task has the controls. How https://every.?ev_audience=free

FIX YOUR FOLDERS

 * A prompt that audits your whole setup. Tell your agent to explain your folder setup and which files are the originals, have Compound Engineering’s ce-doc-review check that explanation, and don’t let your agent move anything without your approval. The prompt https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Four rules from a working setup. Kieran Klaassen https://every.?ev_audience=free keeps one folder per job; stores what his agents know apart from the system that hands them tasks; keeps daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly memory files, and fits the system to how he already works. His setup https://every.?ev_audience=free

SPEND TOKENS ON PURPOSE

 * What 4.5 billion tokens buys. Randy’s unbounded agent swarm ran for a day and a half on one Blender model; the rebuilt setup caps the orchestrator at five subagents and gives a judge agent a reference image. The fix https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * A prompt that audits your token spend. Paste it into your agent to review a session’s usage records, separate necessary work from repeated work and status checks, and recommend three changes. The prompt https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Match the model to the task. Marcus Moretti https://every.?ev_audience=free uses Sonnet https://every.?ev_audience=free for basic checks, Opus https://every.?ev_audience=free for tightly scoped changes, and Fable 5.1 https://every.?ev_audience=free to plan large features; he tells it to delegate coding and check the work.
